controlled_misconceptions.name: Current and Resistance Direct Proportionality
controlled_misconceptions.description: Believes that electric current and resistance are directly proportional (e.g. increasing resistance increases current).
controlled_misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: When the resistor value was doubled, more current flowed through the circuit because resistance increases current.
controlled_misconceptions.example_correct_but_incomplete: Current depends on the resistance value according to Ohm's law.

controlled_misconceptions.name: Resistance Dependent on Current at Constant V
controlled_misconceptions.description: Believes that intrinsic resistance rises when current increases at constant potential difference.
controlled_misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: As more current passes through the conductor at fixed voltage, the resistance of the wire increases.
controlled_misconceptions.example_correct_but_incomplete: Resistance is a property of the wire material and geometry.

controlled_misconceptions.name: Current Consumption in Components
controlled_misconceptions.description: Believes electric current is consumed or 'used up' by components (like bulbs or resistors) as it travels along a series circuit.
controlled_misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: The second bulb is dimmer because the first bulb consumed half the current.
controlled_misconceptions.example_correct_but_incomplete: Current flows through both bulbs in the series circuit.

controlled_misconceptions.name: Voltage Division in Parallel Branches
controlled_misconceptions.description: Believes that potential difference divides equally across parallel branches rather than remaining identical.
controlled_misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: Since there are two parallel branches across a 12V supply, each branch gets 6V.
controlled_misconceptions.example_correct_but_incomplete: Parallel branches share common connection nodes.

controlled_misconceptions.name: Power and Energy Confusion
controlled_misconceptions.description: Confuses electrical power (Watts, rate of energy transfer) with electrical energy (Joules or kWh).
controlled_misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: A 100 Watt appliance consumed 100 Joules total regardless of how long it ran.
controlled_misconceptions.example_correct_but_incomplete: Power is measured in Watts and depends on voltage and current.

controlled_misconceptions.name: No Controlled Misconception
controlled_misconceptions.description: No recognized controlled misconception detected; reasoning is either sound, incomplete, or ambiguous.
controlled_misconceptions.example_wrong_answer: Current decreases because resistance blocks the movement of charge.
controlled_misconceptions.example_correct_but_incomplete: The current changed when voltage changed.
